patient.chief_complaint: First-time witnessed generalized seizure preceded by a strange rising sensation in the stomach and a feeling of deja vu
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Hernandez is a 34-year-old right-handed male physical therapist who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His wife reports that approximately six hours prior to arrival, she observed the patient suddenly stop mid-conversation and stare blankly for about 10 to 15 seconds. He appeared to smack his lips and fumble with his shirt buttons with his right hand. She called his name but he did not respond. He then developed stiffening of all four extremities followed by rhythmic bilateral jerking lasting approximately 90 seconds. He was incontinent of urine during the event. Following the episode, he was confused and drowsy for approximately 30 minutes before gradually returning to his baseline.

Upon interview, the patient recalls that just before the event he experienced an intense feeling of deja vu accompanied by a peculiar rising sensation from his epigastrium toward his throat. He describes having had similar brief episodes of deja vu with the epigastric rising sensation approximately three to four times over the past six months, each lasting 30 to 60 seconds, after which he would feel momentarily disoriented. He attributed these episodes to stress and did not seek medical attention. He denies any prior convulsions, loss of consciousness, or similar episodes in the past other than the febrile seizures in early childhood documented in his medical records. There has been no recent illness, fever, head trauma, sleep deprivation, or changes in medications. He denies any preceding headache, visual changes, or weakness. He has never taken antiepileptic medications.

results.summary: Early surgical intervention for mesial temporal lobe epilepsy resulted in significantly better seizure freedom (73% vs 0%) compared to continued medical therapy at 2 years.

results.title: ILAE consensus on definition of drug-resistant epilepsy
results.summary: Drug-resistant epilepsy defined as failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen, and used AED schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.

output.summary: Current evidence supports early surgical evaluation in patients with mesial temporal sclerosis and drug-resistant focal seizures. The ERSET trial demonstrated superior seizure freedom rates (73% vs 0%) with early surgery compared to continued medical therapy at 2 years. Approximately 52-80% of patients remain seizure-free at 10 years following temporal lobe resection. First-line AED options for focal epilepsy include levetiracetam, lamotrigine, and oxcarbazepine.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of left mesial temporal lobe origin with hippocampal sclerosis (focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with classic mesial-temporal aura)

differential.diagnosis: First unprovoked seizure of unknown etiology
differential.key_features: Without lesional findings would fit; here the aura and MRI HS clarify symptomatic focal epilepsy.
No postural prodrome and prolonged post-ictal confusion are inconsistent.
Adult-onset without prior myoclonus and focal aura argues against.
Labs/history exclude; classic aura suggests true focal epilepsy.
Stereotyped aura with witnessed tonic-clonic activity is not PNES.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura, automatisms, duration, frequency, witness accounts, and post-ictal features.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness events with temporal-lobe aura and post-ictal confusion.
Interictal exam typically normal; subtle memory deficit may be present.

optimal_actions.action: Order EEG (routine first; pursue ambulatory or video-EEG if non-diagnostic) to identify interictal epileptiform discharges and capture habitual events.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Interictal sharps/spikes and/or focal slowing in the anterior temporal region; ictal correlate confirms diagnosis.

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol (thin-cut coronal T1/FLAIR/T2/DWI through the hippocampi).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hippocampal sclerosis, low-grade tumor (DNET, ganglioglioma), cavernoma, or focal cortical dysplasia; rule out alternative structural causes.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, prolactin (if drawn within 10–20 min of event), and AED levels if on therapy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude metabolic provocation (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, uremia); baseline organ function for AED selection; AED level for adherence and dosing.

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature for AED selection in focal epilepsy and ILAE 2017 seizure classification.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evidence-based AED options for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide); ILAE classification framework.

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating or modifying AED therapy (enzyme inducers, OCP, other CNS-active drugs).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify pharmacokinetic interactions (CYP induction by carbamazepine/phenytoin) and CNS adverse-effect overlap.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; CSF analysis is not indicated for routine focal epilepsy workup and exposes the patient to procedural risk and cost.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural-heart concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to epilepsy workup.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; not indicated when semiology is clearly epileptic.
Non-contrast head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting epileptogenic substrates (hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, low-grade tumor) and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural cause influences AED choice (e.g., low-grade tumor → consider AEDs with CYP-neutral profile; hippocampal sclerosis → multiple equally appropriate options). MRI should inform drug selection.

critical_actions: Recognize rising-epigastric sensation with déjà vu as classic mesial-temporal aura.
Obtain routine EEG to look for left anterior temporal sharps or focal slowing.
Obtain 3T MRI with epilepsy protocol to confirm hippocampal sclerosis or alternative substrate.
Initiate a first-line AED (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, or lacosamide).
Counsel on driving restrictions and seizure precautions; address sleep hygiene.
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform LP without specific clinical indication.
Do not start valproate as first-line for confirmed focal epilepsy when better-tolerated options exist.
Do not pursue cardiac workup as the primary etiology in a patient with classic temporal aura.
key_reasoning_points: ILAE criteria for epilepsy diagnosis after a single seizure require ≥60% 10-year recurrence risk — present here given imaging + EEG evidence of structural lesion.
Classic aura semiology + concordant MRI + concordant EEG = high diagnostic confidence.
First-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy includes lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide (ILAE 2017 guideline).
